title: Discover the Ancient Roman Shorthand Writing System with 4,000 Symbols Commissioned by Cicero
description: You can still type a sym­bol orig­i­nal­ly invent­ed for Cicero near­ly 21 cen­turies ago — at least if you con­fig­ure your key­board prop­er­ly
body:
You can still type a sym­bol orig­i­nal­ly invent­ed for Cicero near­ly 21 cen­turies ago — at least if you con­fig­ure your key­board prop­er­ly.  The char­ac­ter ⁊ appears in Uni­code as U+204A, but is bet­ter known as the “Tiron­ian et”: the “et” is Latin for “and,” and the “Tiron­ian” comes from its cre­ator, a man named Tiro, or in full, Mar­cus Tul­lius Tiro. Tiro was­n’t a rel­a­tive of Mar­cus Tul­lius Cicero, as you might expect, but rather his one­time slave: after being eman­ci­pat­ed, he not only took on two of his for­mer mas­ter’s names, but also remained his sec­re­tary and con­fi­dant. It was in that capac­i­ty that, at Cicero’s request, he cre­at­ed the sys­tem since known as Tiron­ian notes.
Though now cred­it­ed as “the father of stenog­ra­phy,” Tiro did­n’t invent short­hand itself. Like so many devel­op­ments in ancient Roman civ­i­liza­tion, Hel­lenic inspi­ra­tion was involved: no soon­er did Cicero learn of the exis­tence of Greek short­hand sys­tems, so the sto­ry goes, than he asked Tiro to come up with one for Latin. It’s pos­si­ble that he did so as ear­ly as 75 BC, when Cicero was assigned to Sici­ly and need­ed to encode his com­mu­ni­ca­tions, espe­cial­ly those hav­ing to do with the cor­rup­tion of local offi­cials. Back in Rome, it became use­ful indeed for rapid­ly tran­scrib­ing onto wax-cov­ered tablets what the great ora­tor had to say, in sit­u­a­tions rang­ing from every­day deal­ings in the Forum to — as record­ed by Plutarch — denounc­ing Cati­line’s con­spir­a­cy to over­throw the Roman Repub­lic.
Tiro cre­at­ed about 4,000 sym­bols to stand in for syl­la­bles, words, and oth­er ele­ments of lan­guage, and oth­er of the sys­tem’s users, includ­ing Seneca, lat­er brought the num­ber up to 5,000. But “as Rome declined, so did short­hand,” writes Ani­ta Kre­itz­man at the Nation­al Court Reporters Asso­ci­a­tion. “The Emper­or Jus­tin­ian, in the sixth cen­tu­ry, con­temp­tu­ous­ly for­bade its use.” Yet Tiron­ian notes sur­vived, espe­cial­ly among the anno­ta­tors of man­u­scripts, expand­ing and merg­ing with oth­er sys­tems to con­tain 14,000 signs dur­ing the Car­olin­gian dynasty. Alas, “Holy Roman Emper­or Fred­er­ick II (1212–1250) con­sid­ered the use of short­hand sym­bols ‘dia­bol­i­cal’ and ‘ordered the destruc­tion of all short­hand char­ac­ters.’ As a result, short­hand quick­ly became a lost art.”
There­upon came the Dark Ages in which “learn­ing and short­hand seemed to no longer exist.” Leave it to court reporters to equate abbre­vi­a­tion with civ­i­liza­tion. Yet the asso­ci­a­tion is hard­ly spu­ri­ous, and can’t be acci­den­tal that its revival began in late six­teenth-cen­tu­ry Lon­don, when the world’s trans­for­ma­tion over the sub­se­quent cen­turies was get­ting into motion. Many short­hand sys­tems have risen and fall­en since, and the dig­i­tal tech­nolo­gies of recent decades have made the whole prac­tice super­flu­ous for most of us here in the twen­ty-first cen­tu­ry. Yet we can still have ⁊, thanks to inad­ver­tent preser­va­tion by the medieval Irish script and Gael­ic type that use it as an amper­sand. It may not have the same func­tion in Eng­lish, or even the Romance lan­guages, but typ­ing no oth­er sym­bol could make us feel quite so Ciceron­ian.
Relat­ed con­tent:
The Code of Charles Dick­ens’ Short­hand Has Been Cracked by Com­put­er Pro­gram­mers, Solv­ing a 160-Year-Old Mys­tery
Alice in Won­der­land, Ham­let, and A Christ­mas Car­ol Writ­ten in Short­hand (Cir­ca 1919)
Behold the Micro­scop­i­cal­ly Tiny Hand­writ­ing of Nov­el­ist Robert Walser, Which Took Four Decades to Deci­pher
The Sto­ry of Lorem Ipsum: How Scram­bled Text by Cicero Became Used by Type­set­ters Every­where
What Ancient Latin Sound­ed Like, And How We Know It
The Writ­ing Sys­tems of the World Explained, from the Latin Alpha­bet to the Abugi­das of India
Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: A New Book Celebrates More Than 250 Trailblazing Women Photographers Across 200 Years
description: In the introduction of a new book titled Great Women Photographers, Fiona Rogers writes, “If ‘greatness’ has long been defined by visibility and r
body:
In the introduction of a new book titled Great Women Photographers, Fiona Rogers writes, “If ‘greatness’ has long been defined by visibility and remembrance, then the continued documentation and celebration of women’s photographic practice is not only relevant but essential.”
The forthcoming title spans a multitude of photographic works from 68 countries and covers nearly 200 years of history. It’s the fourth volume in Phaidon’s series of books commemorating influential women in the artistic sphere, with previous installments focusing on distinct creative mediums such as painting and sculpting.
Alex Prager, “Eve,” 2008. Image courtesy of the artist, Alex Prager Studio, and Lehmann Maupin, New York, Seoul, and London. Chromogenic print, 36 x 45 inches
Highlighting more than 250 women in the field of photography, Great Women Photographers is organized alphabetically by name. Each artist entry includes recently commissioned texts written by leading scholars, accompanied with iconic images from the featured photographers.
From photojournalism and editorial portraiture to cameraless images and conceptual landscapes, Great Women Photographers is not only a visual record of the diverse contributions made by women but also, as the publisher notes, “a new lens on the world, inviting readers to discover, engage with, and be inspired by the work of some of the world’s greatest image-makers.”
You may also enjoy exploring other titles in the series, including Great Women Artists, Great Women Painters, and Great Women Sculptors. Great Women Photographers is slated for release on October 14, 2026. Pre-order your copy in the Colossal Shop. We also have a copy of Great Women Sculptors available now.
Carolle Bénitah, “Le Déguisement (The Disguise),” 2009. Image © Carolle Bénitah, courtesy of Clémentine de la Féronnière Gallery & Sous Les Étoiles Gallery. Archival pigment print with silk thread, 16 1/2 × 24 inches
Simryn Gill, from the series “A Small Town at the Turn of the Century,” 1999–2000. Image courtesy of the artist. Chromogenic print, 36 x 36 inches
Gohar Dashti, “Untitled #5 from the series Today’s Life and War,” 2008. Image courtesy of the artist, shared with permission. Archival pigment print, 27 1/2 × 41 1/2 inches
Pushpamala N., “The Native Types / Circus from the series Native Women of South India,” 2004. Image courtesy of the artist and Nature Morte Delhi. Color photograph, 22 x 1413/16 inches, edition of 20, Art Gallery of New South Wales

title: 11-Year-Old Boy Sets Guinness Record for World’s Youngest Curator
description:
News
                Anderson Taylor opened the Cambridge Natural History Museum in rural Illinois at just nine years old
body:
News
                Anderson Taylor opened the Cambridge Natural History Museum in rural Illinois at just nine years old
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Eleven-year-old Anderson Taylor opened the Cambridge Natural History Museum in August 2024. (all images courtesy Cambridge Natural History Museum)
    
        
            A few weeks shy of his 10th birthday, Anderson Taylor opened a museum in the small town of Cambridge, Illinois, with just one display case. Two years later, after expanding the collection to over a dozen cases of animal fossils, iridescent bones, and rare minerals, Taylor set a Guinness World Record as the world’s youngest museum curator.Announced July 15, the award notes the curator's precise age as nine years and 340 days old when the Cambridge Natural History Museum opened on August 10, 2024.

title: New Digital Archive Honors Gaza Journalists Killed by Israel
description:
News
                The project developed by the Writers Against the War on Gaza serves as a digital memorial for the around 24
body:
News
                The project developed by the Writers Against the War on Gaza serves as a digital memorial for the around 240 Palestinian journalists killed in Gaza since October 2023.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Top (left to right): Mohammed Qraiqea, Anas al-Sharif, Moamen Aliwa; Bottom (left to right): Ayat Khadoura, Mohammed al-Khalidi, Ibrahim Zaher (all images courtesy Writers Against the War on Gaza (WAWOG) unless otherwise noted)
    
        
            “Anas was one of the journalists who ran into the line of fire,” reads a translated eulogy by independent journalist Doaa Shaheen about her late colleague, prominent Al Jazeera reporter Anas al-Sharif, 28, who was killed alongside four other journalists on August 10, 2025, by a targeted Israeli strike on their media tent near al-Shifa Hospital. “He covered events as they unfolded because he believed the Palestinian narrative was worth this effort and exhaustion,” Shaheen's voice note continued. “Our stories are worth all this suffering. They deserve our presence on the front lines, documenting the truth.”Shaheen's oral eulogy is one of several devoted to al-Sharif on a new digital memorial for Gaza's martyred journalists. Developed and launched by the Writers Against the War on Gaza (WAWOG) yesterday, August 12, “The Living Record” is an oral archive for remembering and recognizing the small but extraordinarily endangered community of Palestinian reporters, especially as the number of Gaza press fatalities by Israel since October 2023 hovers at around 240. The Living Record launched with individual memorial pages for 24 slain journalists. Profiles and eulogies for another 21 journalists will be added throughout the fall, and the archive will continue to grow in acknowledgment of the historically high yield of targeted press fatalities during the Gaza genocide.

title: The Artist Mapping Knoxville’s Art Scene With Wood and Wire
description:
Feature

body:
Feature
                Three years ago, Lauren Farkas sketched a plan to see exhibitions during the city’s monthly art walk. Now, she crafts eclectic maps for each event to make the art scene more accessible.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
                
        
            Lauren Farkas, “Sign Map” (2024), wire-traced carving into a reflective 48-inch road sign with electrical tape and clock overlay/axis (all photos courtesy the artist, unless otherwise noted)
    
        
            KNOXVILLE, Tenn. — On the first Friday of each month, a dozen or more exhibitions open across galleries, studios, and temporary spaces in Knoxville. For many people in the small city’s art community, the night is either an overwhelming jumble or a repetitive routine. Artist Lauren Farkas’s maps offer a way through.“If everything is on the map, people get overwhelmed,” Farkas told Hyperallergic. “I put all the things that I would like to go to if I had enough time on the map.”Farkas, a high school art teacher at L&N STEM Academy who has lived in Knoxville for nine years, said that she considers her educational work to be “a long-form performance piece.” She approaches each map as an artwork with a similar sense of structure: The geography remains fixed, while the shows and events shift from month to month.Anchored by the Knoxville Museum of Art (KMA) and the University of Tennessee School of Art, the city's arts ecosystem extends beyond downtown’s familiar gallery circuit to include a growing network of artist-run spaces, community studios, and exhibitions that many attendees might otherwise overlook.Lauren Farkas, “Glove Map” (2025), needle-felted into sewn glovesFarkas has used watercolor, tape, and digital animation, among other forms, to craft First Friday maps that help people make sense of the evening’s many possibilities — and feel confident exploring them. “It’s an invitation, especially for people who might not otherwise feel they belong in those spaces,” Farkas explained.One map transformed a pair of white sneakers into a walking guide, with Knoxville’s streets and gallery locations etched directly into the soles so that each step echoed the idea of an “art walk.” Another was made entirely from locally harvested materials — paper mulberry pulp, goldenrod, black walnut ink, acorns, and charred wood — creating, as Farkas describes it, “a map of the place with the place.”For Kelsie Conley, assistant curator at the KMA, the maps transcend the role of an ordinary event guide. “They slow us down and change the way we experience the city,” she said. “They still do the practical work of helping us move through the city, but the information becomes something you have to spend time with. They ask us to think about the city as something that is felt, rather than just a fixed collection of destinations.”Farkas making her “Kudzu Ecollage” (2024), kudzu and pen on torn kudzu labels (photo courtesy Chelsie Nunn)Lauren Farkas, “Footprint Map” (2026), burned map lines into soles of sneakers, installation with crayons and papers for interactive texture rubbing activityThe maps began as a way to orient Farkas herself in the city’s vibrant arts scene. Three years ago, she was sitting at her desk, scrolling through her phone, and making a plan for the evening. She sketched a map for herself in colored pencil — an attempt to make sense of First Fridays and get to as many shows as possible, thinking her way through time and space. She shared it on her Instagram story. A few friends started referencing it, and a project took shape.“It was useful for me, and someone else used it,” Farkas said. “I thought, ‘Maybe that’s a need or a deficit in the local art world here.’”Farkas continued creating simple maps over the next few months, posting them to her Instagram story. Around month four or five, she tried using different materials — watercolors led to markers, embroidery, wood ash, gouache on vellum, and even a double-sided shadow lamp.Her audience is not easy to track, and she doesn’t always know who is using the maps. Some follow along through her Substack; others may just learn about her work through word of mouth.Lauren Farkas, “Circuit Map” (2025), scavenged coaxial cable, aluminum tape, embedded LED circuitsThe maps have already changed how people experience First Friday; Conley also credits them with flattening the boundaries within Knoxville’s art scene. “There’s no hierarchy to them,” she said. Whether it’s an exhibition at a major gallery or in someone’s apartment, Farkas treats them as equally worthy of attention. Artist Josh Shorey describes First Friday as “a tradition and a distributed network” — a monthly event that has evolved organically, without a central organizing body. When a photographer who had recently moved to Knoxville from Los Angeles asked him how First Friday worked, Shorey found himself pulling up one of Farkas’s maps to explain it.“Doing this for every First Friday builds a culture,” said Farkas. “It helps build consistency. I want people to see the value and interconnectedness of everything happening on First Friday.”Lauren Farkas with Kyle Cottier, “Curtain Map: A Map Is a Thing You Walk Through” (2025), alcohol markers applied with an airbrush tool on maple, strung togetherLauren Farkas, “Clay Slab Texture Rubbing Map” (2024), carved clay slab with multicolor chalk pastel rubbingLauren Farkas with Daniel Clay, “Tilt Maze Map” (2025), medium-density fiberboard (MDF), cut and carved with a computer numerical control (CNC) router

title: A View From the Easel
description: Welcome to the 350th installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Linda Lay set
body:
Welcome to the 350th installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Linda Lay sets up shop in the mobile home she grew up in, collapsing time and tenderly reclaiming the space through her vibrant art practice.Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.Linda Lay, Marina, CaliforniaHow long have you been working in this space?Three years.Describe an average day in your studio.An average day in my studio begins around 10 in the morning, as I’m most productive at the start of the day, and although I rise early, I like to first have coffee with my partner at home, which is nearby. In my main working areas I have little “stations” where I keep projects-in-progress, often with supplies close at hand, so that I can get right to it. I allow myself the freedom to start with whatever feels natural in the moment, as I know that will lead me to working on whatever has a deadline.In art school, one of my professors observed that my “starting routine” for making art is something like what a dog does when they lie down for a nap — how they move around in circles on their bed until it feels right to settle in. I’m still very much that way, figuratively, of course.The first thing I do when I enter the studio is open the windows for airflow and light. I then walk around to say “hello” to the space and plants, and if I feel the need to, I safely light some sage. I always burn incense as this helps me feel like I'm setting some sort of "intention" for the day. I often listen to podcasts or audiobooks once I get settled into working. (I love Fashion Neurosis by Bella Freud.) When I was busy converting this mobile home, which I was raised in, into my art studio, I was listening more to music from eras of my past that I may have listened to when I was a child and teenager, or what I listened to when I moved away from home at the start of the ’90s.How does the space affect your work?The space affects my work in two different ways: In one way, it’s the first time I’ve had a full art studio outside of home or shared studios. I have a lot of stuff from the past hung up at the moment, combined with newer pieces and projects. I’m able to be with it all in a way that’s private, and this is important to me. It helps my focus tremendously.The second way the space affects my work is that it was once my childhood home, and it wasn’t a positive space. I didn’t know what to expect when I was given the freedom to make changes that I had so wished I could change as a child. Being in this very specific place, and having been able to change it without worry of perfect construction or traditional interior design rules, has made the space itself a very personal conceptual artwork.I work in an intuitive manner with a lot of craft-inspired processes that mirror how things are made while being raised in poverty, which I was. Many of my artistic concepts have to do with synchronicities occurring in space and time, so it’s like I’m “communicating” with the past in a very direct way.How do you interact with the environment outside your studio?The literal environment outside of my studio is the mobile home park I used to play in as a child in the ’80s. It was a great place to be, and I had fantastic friends. There was a playground and we used to stay outside all day long. I have an incredible memory of wandering around the park, giggling with my pals as pre-teens while the Live Aid concert was being televised. We'd occasionally leave our televisions in order to pretend to flirt with a cute boy who was visiting his grandparents for the summer. It's been great to consider moments like this while working on my art. There are two older women still there who I knew back then, the mothers of kids who were my friends. These older women are immigrants who were hard-working, like my own mother was. They often knock on my door and bring me food and check in. It’s very warm and comforting.I am connected to the art community here on the Monterey Peninsula, and for the past three years I’ve been organizing and hosting a private monthly art salon, which has been great. Everyone must perceive their art as something more than a hobby.There are people in my community who are focused on art in a big way — who are exploring many different concepts and work in varied practices and mediums. I returned to the area after living in Los Angeles for many years, and I’ve found my community here through hosting my salon and by attending local art and literary events. It’s a bit difficult to sift through the “sell art to tourists” mentality out here, but there is definitely more to be found.What do you love about your studio?I love that I have a history with and connection to my studio, and that I have made it something special. I love that I set parameters on spending money on materials when I was fixing it up. I visited a local charity shop that offers free, donated house paint. I got so many great colors from there, for free!I love that I decided to play and “listen” to the space in keeping certain family mementos, plants, and objects in my work areas. I love that the studio itself is a work of art and that it has a story.I am in heaven over the fact that I have space to make as well as space for my work to hang, as I have a specific aesthetic that isn't always easy to showcase with the works of others, especially in my community.I love that I can finally have proper studio visits.What do you wish were different?I wish I had more parking available. We are only allowed one spot, and street parking is always taken.What is your favorite local museum?We don't have a lot of options outside of all things having to do with John Steinbeck, early California history, and the Monterey Bay Aquarium, so I'll say the Monterey Museum of Art. They showcase California art, and for a smallish town, they were able to swing a David Hockney exhibition in 2019 with mostly his iPad works depicting Yosemite. They support local artists, engage with the community, and they sometimes challenge our expectations, which doesn’t always happen here.What is your favorite art material to work with?Fiber materials are my favorite.

title: The Guggenheim Wants Its Picasso Back
description:
Daily Newsletter
                The museum sues for ownership of a Picasso painting stolen in 1961, plus new affordable housing
body:
Daily Newsletter
                The museum sues for ownership of a Picasso painting stolen in 1961, plus new affordable housing for artists in Philly.
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            In 1961, a painting by Pablo Picasso on loan from the Guggenheim Museum mysteriously vanished from the University of Pittsburgh. This week, the museum filed a lawsuit to get it back. Senior Editor Valentina Di Liscia has the scoop on the rediscovery and where it’s been for the last six decades.In other rediscovered painting news, Staff Writer Anna Lee reports on a 17th-century Flemish still life that surfaced after years lost in storage at the National Museum of Norway, where it will soon be correctly attributed to artist Clara Peeters for the first time.More below, including Art Movements, Required Reading, and some of the best films on art and resistance that critic Elodie Saint-Louis and I saw at the unparalleled BlackStar Film Festival in Philadelphia last weekend. Coincidentally, BlackStar shares an office building with the Village of Industry & Art, a nonprofit that plans to transform the city’s shuttered dorm rooms into affordable apartment units. As loyal as I am to Pittsburgh, I gotta say, Philly’s art scene is cooking.—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor


	
		
			A Picasso Vanished in 1961. The Guggenheim Now Wants It Back
		
	
	
		The Picasso had disappeared without a trace.

On the morning of February 6, 1961, a graduate student and dormitory aide at the University of Pittsburgh reported Picasso’s painting “Femme dans un fauteuil” (1918) missing from the Students Union building. The 13.5-by-10.5-inch oil had been on loan from the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation for an exhibition in the fall semester, and was due to be returned to the museum later that month. The school reported the theft to the Pittsburgh Police Department and the FBI was swiftly brought in to investigate, but despite a slew of news articles, notifications to institutions across North America, and a reward for information, the case went cold.

More than six decades later, the Guggenheim says the painting has turned up, and it is headed to court to get it back. | Valentina Di Liscia
	
	
		Read More
	

NewsThe Village of Industry & Art will transform a dormitory in a former Philly UArts building into 45 affordable units for artists by fall 2027.A long-misattributed painting is set to resurface in a forthcoming exhibition  at the National Museum of Norway, where it will be publicly attributed to the Flemish painter Clara Peeters for the first time.Art Movements: New leaders at the Portland Art Museum and Storm King Art Center, the new cohort of fellows at ISLAA, the bittersweet closure of a West Coast arts magazine, Mamdani’s plans for Elizabeth Street Garden, and more. 		This week: Nancy Spero’s pro-choice art, Valentina Di Liscia on “Casa Cueva,” Brooklyn’s smallest museum, Jamaica Kincaid’s eyebrows, Israeli cuisine and Palestinian erasure, and more.
